newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Anti-communist hero sees more trouble in Albania.
newsitem.headline: Anti-communist hero sees more trouble in Albania.

text.p: Azem Hajdari, revolutionary student leader turned trade union boss, on Thursday predicted more trouble in Albania unless a new government stepped in to resolve a worsening crisis over failed pyramid schemes.

Hajdari, who led protests at Tirana university in the 1990 revolt that ousted the hardline communists, said protests were bound to escalate when thousands discover they will not get all their cash back from the crumbling investment funds.
"If the government is not changed, and if people don't get their money back, I do not know what is going to happen but I am very pessimistic," Hajdari told Reuters in an interview.
"There are no political forces that will be able to keep the crowds under control," he said.

Western governments and the United States, in particular, should put heavy pressure on Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi's government to halt a further plunge into a financial and political abyss, he added.

Police prevented Hajdari, who is also a member of parliament, from holding a rally in Tirana on Wednesday, and during the interview he was handed a letter from police authorities turning down his request for a fresh demonstration.

"If they keep preventing trade unions from holding legal protests, then we shall have to start marches in the streets...or go on strike," said Hajdari, who heads an independent trade union with around 130,000 members.
Police blocked students from joining his demonstration on Wednesday and if pressure continued, he said, they too will come out into the streets.
Trade union leaders decided against pushing for the protest to go ahead to avoid bloody clashes with security forces but Hajdari stressed there was a limit to the workers' patience.

Industrial workers were paid a pittance and were among the thousands who had lost out badly in the failed pyramid schemes. Students were also suffering under terrible conditions, including poor lighting, heating and food on campus.

Albania's opposition had been fragmented and weakened by in-fighting but on Thursday seven parties, including the big Socialist Party, launched a Forum for Democracy alliance, which could spearhead more organised protests against the government.
Hajdari, who co-founded the Democratic Party in 1990 with President Sali Berisha and others, said he had not ruled out talking to the new forum to discuss a united front.

He said the government was trying to create the impression of "red terror", blaming leftists and former members of the communist Sigurimi secret police for the wave of unrest, but people from all walks of life and political persuasion were affected by the pyramids scandal and had a right to protest.

The Interior Ministry said some 247 people were helping police with their inquiries over the torching of government buildings in the south. Socialists say hundreds more have been rounded up in what amounted to political intimidation.

Hajdari described Berisha as a genuine liberal but whose power was being eroded by a corrupt core of Democrats. The president was also further weakened by constitutional rules barring him from dissolving parliament or sacking the government six months before he stands for re-election.
Parliament elects the president and Berisha must stand for election in April.
Hajdari also said another alternative to the crisis would be changes inside the Democratic Party but declined to say whether he foresaw a split or a government ouster from within.
